name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,786

clue.text: Mean spirited type might need organ replaced

indicators.note: put back in different places, so the letters change position

explanation.surface: A doctor muses that a nasty piece of work might need a transplant, a new heart perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is built on 'heartless': 'organ replaced' reads as surgery, but it is three whole words of fodder plus the signal to rearrange them.
explanation.definitionFit: From the fable of the dog lying in hay it cannot eat so the ox cannot either: a person who spitefully keeps from others what is no use to himself.

clue.text: One's responsible for housing issue after the folks have departed

definitions.text: One's responsible for housing issue after the folks have departed

blocks.note: read as a council office handling a housing problem; meant as a place that gives a home to someone's issue, their children
read as residents moving out; meant as the parents, one's folks, having died

explanation.surface: An official deals with a housing problem once the residents have moved out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' is the pivot: the surface makes it a problem, the clue means offspring, and 'departed' is the old euphemism for dead.
explanation.definitionFit: An institution that takes in and houses children whose parents have died is exactly this.

clue.text: Chris Lambert keeps faith

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, as the name holds the answer across its two words

blocks.note: chrIS LAMbert, running across the gap between first name and surname

explanation.surface: A man called Chris Lambert stays true to his religion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeps faith' reads as a set phrase meaning stays loyal, which hides that 'keeps' is doing the containing.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a faith is a religion, and this is the religion of Muslims.

clue.text: Keen teenager's outside entrance

indicators.note: the outside of a word is its two end letters, with the inside thrown away

blocks.note: the verb, stressed on the second syllable: to entrance is to enchant

explanation.surface: An eager youngster is standing by the door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entrance' reads as a doorway, and 'Keen' as eager; both are other senses, a verb and sharpness.
explanation.definitionFit: Keen in the sense of sharp or cutting, as a keen or trenchant wit is.

clue.text: Great golfer periodically upset scorer

indicators.note: at regular periods, so every second letter is taken
set upside down, which in a down entry turns the letters to read from the bottom

blocks.note: the even letters of gReAt GoLfEr

explanation.surface: A top golfer has a bad day and knocks over the player who is scoring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scorer' suggests the golf scorecard; it is someone who writes musical scores.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossword pun: Edward Elgar, the English composer of the Enigma Variations, wrote scores, so he is a scorer.

clue.text: Type of software creating Sun trivia

indicators.note: to create is to make something new, so the letters are made into a new word

explanation.surface: A program churns out trivia for The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make Sun the newspaper, but only its three letters matter here.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by class: antivirus is one type of software, the kind that guards a computer against malicious code.

clue.text: Complaint initially gives Richard Osman anxious nights

indicators.note: at the start of each word, so the first letters are taken

explanation.surface: A grumble keeps the TV quiz host and novelist Richard Osman awake at night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' could be an illness here, the kind that brings anxious nights; it is a grumble.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a groan is a moan of complaint, the noise of someone grumbling.

clue.text: Revolutionary head shows sign of embarrassment

blocks.note: a red is a revolutionary, from the red flag
a ness is a headland, as in many British place names

explanation.surface: A rebel leader blushes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary head' reads as one leader; the two words are separate pieces, and 'head' is a headland.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: a flush of colour in the cheeks is the sign someone is embarrassed.

clue.text: At heart of row carrying on without a break

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle letter
to carry is to hold something, so two pieces hold another between them

blocks.note: in cricket the on side is also called the leg side

explanation.surface: In the middle of an argument someone keeps going without pausing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carrying on' reads as a phrase meaning continuing; split it. Cricket's leg side, facing the batsman's legs, is the on side.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical term: legato tells a player to join the notes smoothly, without a break between them.

clue.text: Banish not entirely fair English Liberal

indicators.note: not the entire word, so its last letter is missing

blocks.note: EXPO (a trade fair) without its last letter

explanation.surface: A not-quite-fair decision throws out an English Liberal politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair' reads as just; it is a noun, an exhibition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to banish someone is to drive them out, as a school might.

clue.text: Rowers go under multiple times

blocks.note: a racing crew of eight oarsmen is itself called an eight
a failing business folds, or goes under

explanation.surface: A rowing crew keeps capsizing again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go under' sounds like sinking, which suits rowers; here it is a business failing.
explanation.definitionFit: Eight times over is one particular multiple, so the definition is a loose description of a specific number of times.

clue.text: Recurrent cold - I intend acting sickly

indicators.note: literally running back, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, as on a tap
a. = acting, as in a job title

explanation.surface: Someone with a cold that keeps coming back says they plan to act ill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recurrent' belongs to the cold in the surface but tells you to read the whole string backwards. ANAEMIC is the British spelling of anemic.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone short of red blood cells looks pale and weak, so the word stretches to mean sickly in general.

clue.text: Say, I don't believe you brought round something like gazpacho?

indicators.note: turned right round, so the letters face the other way

blocks.note: the exclamation you make in disbelief

explanation.surface: A host brings round a cold soup and a guest can't believe it.
explanation.walkthrough: Gazpacho is a Spanish soup served cold, and the proverb says the answer is a dish best served cold; the question mark flags that sideways link.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb calls it a dish best served cold, so it is 'something like' a cold soup.

clue.text: Elegant young socialite leaves broadcasting

indicators.note: the socialite walks out of the word, taking her letters with her

blocks.note: a deb (debutante) is a young woman entering society; she is removed from the front

explanation.surface: A stylish debutante walks out of a TV studio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' could be a noun, but it is the verb, and what departs is the whole of a short word, not a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective used of a programme or presenter being transmitted live at that moment, as on the studio's red sign.

clue.text: Roger Dean playing harmonium perhaps

indicators.note: playing about with the letters rearranges them

explanation.surface: A musician called Roger Dean plays, maybe on a harmonium.
explanation.walkthrough: The name looks like a performer in the scene; it is only a bag of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a harmonium sounds by air passing over metal reeds, so it is one kind of this instrument, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: They'll swear if Republican frames rogue

indicators.note: as an adjective, rogue means out of control, gone astray, so the letters stray out of order

explanation.surface: People will curse if a Republican politician stitches up a rogue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frames' and 'rogue' look like a crime story, a rogue being framed; FRAMES is fodder and 'rogue' the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who affirm make a solemn declaration in court in place of an oath, so they swear in effect.

clue.text: Display of passion does the trick

blocks.note: something that works does the trick

explanation.surface: A show of strong feeling gets the result someone wanted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Display of passion' reads as one phrase, and could even define the answer in its sense of an angry outburst; the definition is just 'Display'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pyrotechnic show on Bonfire Night or New Year is a display, and the word is also used of a heated outburst.

clue.text: Heather comes over drunk with ecstasy - few people know about this

definitions.note: the answer is a plural noun; the clue's 'this' treats it as one body of knowledge

indicators.note: the heather comes over to join the others, arriving last in the line

blocks.note: Erica is the botanical name for heather

explanation.surface: A woman named Heather drops by, drunk and high on ecstasy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heather' looks like a woman's name; it is the plant. 'Drunk' is a noun, a sot.
explanation.definitionFit: Esoteric knowledge is meant for an inner circle only, and the plural noun names such obscure things.

clue.text: Yeoman of the Guard live performance amid unbridled jeers

indicators.note: in the middle of, so one piece sits inside the other
a bridle goes round a horse's head; without it, the letters at each end come off

blocks.note: to live = to be, to exist
a feat is a notable performance

explanation.surface: A Tower of London guard performs live while the crowd jeers wildly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Live performance' reads as one gig; split it, and read 'live' as the verb. 'Unbridled' looks like unrestrained but strips the ends off a word.
explanation.definitionFit: The popular nickname for the Yeomen of the Guard and the Yeomen Warders, the ceremonial guards at the Tower of London.

clue.text: Swaggering Virginia bolsters underwear before party

indicators.note: to bolster is to prop up from underneath, so in a down entry Virginia sits below the underwear

explanation.surface: A cocky woman named Virginia pads out her bra before a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swaggering' looks like an adjective but is the noun here, the act of swaggering, so it can stand for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a loud, swaggering show of boldness meant to impress.

clue.text: For superficial reasons they belittle senior boss regularly

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken and the rest skipped

blocks.note: the odd letters of SeNiOr BoSs

explanation.surface: Staff routinely mock their top manager for shallow reasons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' reads as routinely, the staff's habit, rather than an instruction to take every other letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: people who look down on others over class, taste or money judge on superficial grounds.

clue.text: Originally dropped, Mo Kudus performs! It requires thinking outside the box

definitions.text: It requires thinking outside the box

indicators.note: the original, or first, letter is dropped
the letters put on a show, moving about into a new order

blocks.note: MO with its first letter dropped

explanation.surface: The Ghanaian footballer Mohammed Kudus plays an inventive game after being dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: Mo Kudus is a Ghana international footballer, so 'dropped' reads as left out of the team.
explanation.definitionFit: A joke on the cliche: in this number puzzle the grid is made of boxes, and the thinking happens both inside and across them.

clue.text: Theologian got high with a doctor

explanation.surface: A religious scholar got stoned alongside a physician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got high' suggests drugs; it just means went up.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: St Ambrose, fourth-century bishop of Milan, is one of the Doctors of the Church.

clue.text: Just after going inside teacher had sex with American

indicators.note: one piece goes into the other
tells you the definition is US slang

blocks.note: BEd, Bachelor of Education, a teaching degree
as in 'on the hour', exactly when it strikes

explanation.surface: A scandal: straight after going in, a teacher slept with an American.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Teacher' gives the qualification, not a person. 'American' seems to be the partner in the scene but only flags the slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A vulgar American slang sense of the verb bone is to have sex with someone.

clue.text: Insert key

blocks.note: a verb: to put data in
a noun: a named key on a computer keyboard

explanation.walkthrough: Both words also name keyboard keys, which makes the clue look like a pair of keys rather than a verb and a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To type something in is to insert it, and the key that submits a line is labelled with this word.

clue.text: We finish entertaining street in fashionable area

indicators.note: to entertain is to have guests in, so one piece holds another

explanation.surface: We wind up a street party in a smart part of town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entertaining' suits the answer doubly, as London's theatre district.
explanation.definitionFit: London's district of theatres, shops and smart addresses has long been the city's fashionable side.

clue.text: Southern fliers ignoring female circling up above

indicators.note: to ignore something is to leave it out, so the F for female is dropped
to circle something is to go round it, so these letters surround the next piece

blocks.note: RAF, the Royal Air Force, without F for female

explanation.surface: Pilots from the south fly round overhead, leaving a woman behind.
explanation.walkthrough: Two pieces join to do the circling, so 'Southern' and the fliers wrap round the word between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latin word used in English writing to mean earlier in the text, as in 'see supra'.

clue.text: She denies retired degenerate period heading sports body

definitions.note: 'She' stands for a person, so 'She denies' means one who denies

indicators.note: drawn back, as from a battle, so the letters are read backwards
to head something is to go in front of it

explanation.surface: A woman denies that a retired sports chief had a period of decline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' applies to the whole chain, not the first word: build all three pieces in order, then turn the lot round.
explanation.definitionFit: One who abnegates renounces or denies, and 'She' is the setter's way of turning the verb into an agent.

clue.text: Sober singer steals heart of merry groom

indicators.note: a thief takes something and hides it about their person, so the singer holds the letter
the heart of a word is its middle letter

blocks.note: the US pop singer P!nk, who has spoken of giving up drink

explanation.surface: A teetotal singer upstages a tipsy bridegroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groom' is the verb, not the man at the wedding, and 'merry' (tipsy) is set against 'sober'.
explanation.definitionFit: An old verb for dressing up or smartening oneself, much as a bird preens.

clue.text: He's still not able in the main

definitions.text: He's still not able in the main

blocks.note: read as someone still incapable; meant as a sailor not yet promoted to Able Seaman
read as mostly; meant as at sea, the main being the ocean

explanation.walkthrough: 'The main' is an old word for the open sea, as in the Spanish Main.
explanation.definitionFit: The Royal Navy's lowest rating for a sailor, the rank held before promotion to Able Seaman.
